title: Writing an Even as a Double

steps.body: Every even number can be written as a double: split it into two equal groups and name the sum, like 14 = 7 + 7.
steps.narration: Every even number can be written as a double: split it into two equal groups and name the sum, like 14 = 7 + 7.

widget.prompt: Pair up 18 counters. Odd or even?
widget.oddFeedback: 18 pairs up completely (9 pairs, 0 left). No leftover means even.
widget.successFeedback: Yes — 18 makes 9 pairs with none left over.

predict.reveal: 10 + 8 reaches 18 but the groups differ — a double demands two equal nines.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents g2a even equation.
invariants: Rearranging counters into pairs, rows, or columns changes the VIEW of a quantity, never its count — the model and the total must agree for g2a even equation.
misconceptions: Believing a taller or wider arrangement holds more, or that a leftover counter can be ignored when judging parity.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What single change to the arrangement would change what the number IS, not just how it looks?

explanationVariants: Equal is what makes it a double.

widget.prompt: Which addition shows 14 as a double?

options.feedback: Correct — 14 split into two equal groups of 7 is exactly what "double" means.
That reaches 14, but the parts differ — a double needs two EQUAL addends.
That doubles 14 itself, giving 28 — the question doubles a smaller number to REACH 14.
Unequal parts and one short of 14 — equal groups of 7 are needed.

hints: So a double is always even.

widget.prompt: What kind of number is an odd number plus an odd number?

options.label: even
options.feedback: Correct — an odd number plus an odd number pairs every leftover, so the sum always lands even.

options.label: odd
options.feedback: Try 3 + 5 or 4 + 6: the leftovers pair with each other, leaving none — that is even, not odd.

options.label: sometimes even, sometimes odd
options.feedback: Parity here never wavers — the leftover structure forces the same result every single time.

options.label: impossible to know
options.feedback: You can know without computing: track the leftovers and the parity is decided.

hints: Track the leftovers, not the totals.

widget.prompt: Maggie un-doubles 12: she asks which number, taken twice, rebuilds it. Which addition is she looking for?

options.feedback: Correct — un-doubling 12 finds 6, because 6 taken twice rebuilds 12.
That doubles 12 into 24 — un-doubling asks what was doubled to MAKE 12.
That reaches 12, but 5 and 7 are not the same number taken twice.
3 taken twice rebuilds only 6 — that un-doubles 12 one step too far.
